cells.tense: Something shifted in you a while back and you've been keeping it steady ever since, on purpose, with your eyes open.
cells.ask: Hand one thing you've worked out — a method, a way of reading a situation — to someone who could use it today, and watch what they do with it.
cells.core:
When this part of you is working, you take what came out of something that ended and you put it where it can be used. A friend asks how you handled a thing and you give them the actual shape of it, not the story around it. Seeing the pattern and passing it on is one motion for you; it doesn't sit in a drawer.

Lately you've been keeping it close and passing it on less. You check that the thing is still there, still true, still yours — and the checking feels like care. Up to a point it is. But a pattern stays true where it's used, and the exchange you'd get from offering it — someone's hands doing something you didn't plan — is the one thing guarding it can't give you. Today, once, put it in someone else's hands and find out.
cells.sheetLine: You've found something worth keeping, and the next move is to give it once and see.
cells.verb: hold what the change left standing
cells.place: where you see how things work once the details fall away

cells.tense: You're braced for what might disturb this next, and your grip has tightened to match.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're holding and leave it alone for a day — no checking it, no adjusting it, no explaining it to anyone — and notice what it does without you.
cells.core:
What you have turns into something you're stretched toward defending. Threats show up in your head before they show up in the room, and you patch the thing you understood until the understanding is mostly scaffolding. The pattern you once saw cleanly is now a pattern you maintain, and maintaining it uses the same attention that could be seeing something new.

Keeping it that way doesn't last. What lasts comes from letting what you know meet someone else's read of it. Not losing it — meeting it. Another person who sees it their own way is the only thing that can keep a pattern honest, because they can hold it with you. Loosen one grip today and let another person's look at it land. Whatever's still there after that was the part that was real.
cells.sheetLine: You're guarding the pattern instead of seeing it, and guarding is a different job.

cells.tense: Something settled a while back and you're standing near where it landed, not carrying the shape of it forward.
cells.ask: Write one sentence about something that changed and what you now know because of it, then read it to one person — not to explain, just to put it in the air.
cells.core:
The pattern is there, but you're not doing anything with it. Someone asks what you've taken from it and you answer in generalities, or you turn the question, or you say you haven't really thought about it. Noticing how things work and saying so used to be a habit; now you follow what other people point out instead of pointing it out yourself.

Insight isn't the problem. You're standing at a door that already closed behind you, and the standing is the whole of it. The way forward isn't more thinking. It's picking one thing worth saying and saying it on purpose — one person, one sentence, today, in whatever words come. Not polished, not general. Said.
cells.sheetLine: You saw something that mattered, and you've gone quiet about it. Say one piece today.

cells.tense: You're already shaping what happens around you from this — the pattern carries weight in what you do — and you talk about it like weather.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're keeping in place for other people — a routine, a standard, a way of doing something — and say plainly that you're the one who holds it there.
cells.core:
You notice how something works and then quietly shape what happens next, and you do it without calling it yours. You adjust the routine, you set the standard, you make the shape of a thing visible to whoever needs it — and when it's going well you describe it as just how things are. The influence is real and moving. The saying-so isn't happening.

What you're keeping came out of something ending or changing, and you found the structure in it and held it upright. That's not passive. It's what you actually do — take what's been through the fire and give it a form that stands. Saying so isn't boasting. It's the accurate sentence, and it gives the people around you something solid, because they'll know where it comes from. One sentence today, to yourself or out loud, about one thing you're the one keeping in place.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping the structure standing. Say that's what you're doing.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is any statement about what the person actually holds or what change produced it — the record gives the mechanism, not the content, so the core stays with the holding and the form, not with what's inside. A reader could reasonably say the pattern-seeing is not creating a stability problem in their life; the ask is still useful then, because writing down one thing they're keeping is a small experiment that teaches them whether they're holding or stalling. The sentence that serves the writer most is any line that sounds like a verdict on the person's whole way of living; I've kept the claims narrow enough that they can be refused without losing the reading.
